title: Entity–Relationship Model
relevance: ER modeling is the usual way SDE interviews and OAs ask candidates to express conceptual database design before any storage mapping.

phases.goal: Establish what the ER model is and how entities, attributes, and relationships describe a domain.

must_hit.point: The ER model is a high-level model for designing a database; it describes a domain in terms of entities, attributes, and relationships, and captures logical design (the conceptual schema) without committing to storage details.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States ER is for conceptual/logical design via entities, attributes, and relationships, not physical storage.

must_hit.point: An entity is an object of interest; the entity type (its schema) fixes the structure shared by all such entities.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates a particular entity instance from the entity type that defines the shared structure.

must_hit.point: A relationship is an association between entities.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines relationship as an association and can illustrate with Student studies Course.

probes: What does the ER model describe, and how does it relate to the conceptual schema?

hints.1: Think about designing a database before choosing how data is stored.
hints.2: Name the three building blocks the ER model uses to describe a domain.
hints.3: ER uses entities, attributes, and relationships; it is the language of the conceptual schema without storage details.

phases.goal: Cover ER diagram notation and the independent dimensions used to classify attributes.

must_hit.point: In ER diagrams, a rectangle denotes an entity, an ellipse denotes an attribute, and a diamond denotes a relationship; lines connect attributes to their entity and entities to the relationships they participate in.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly maps rectangle/ellipse/diamond and mentions the connecting lines.

must_hit.point: Attributes are classified along six dimensions: single-valued versus multivalued, simple versus composite, stored versus derived, key versus non-key, required versus optional, and complex (composite and multivalued together).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all six dimensions and states that complex means composite and multivalued combined.

must_hit.point: Multivalued attributes are drawn as a double ellipse, derived attributes as a dashed ellipse, and key attributes are shown underlined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions double ellipse for multivalued, dashed ellipse for derived, and underline for key.

must_hit.point: A simple attribute cannot be subdivided, while a composite attribute decomposes into meaningful parts; a stored attribute is kept as-is, while a derived attribute is computed from others; a required attribute must always carry a value, while an optional one may be left empty; a single-valued attribute holds exactly one value per entity, while a multivalued attribute may hold several.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives correct brief contrasts for simple/composite, stored/derived, required/optional, and single-valued/multivalued.

probes: How are entities, attributes, and relationships drawn, and how do you mark multivalued, derived, and key attributes?

hints.1: Start with the three basic shapes used in an ER diagram.
hints.2: Then say which special ellipse styles mark multivalued versus derived attributes, and how keys are marked.
hints.3: Rectangle = entity, ellipse = attribute, diamond = relationship; double ellipse = multivalued, dashed ellipse = derived, underline = key.
